full_judgment:
Mohammed Habibur Rahman, J.- This  appeal arises out of the judgment and order passed on .5.6.83 by the Subordinate judge, Cox's Bazar in Misc. Case No. 6 of 4981 allowing an application for pre-emption under section 96 of  the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 2. On 14.7.81 pre-emptor respondents 1-3 Mohammad Islam, Kala Mia and Feroza Khatun of village Tetia, P.S. Cox's Bazar filed an application stating that Jyoti Prisad Rakshit and Tarun Tapan Rakshit (sons of late Barada Prasad Rakshit) of village Jayara, P.S. Chand Naish, Patiya, Chittagong sold 7.44. acre of Nal land out of 19.90 acre of land in R.S. plot Nos. 284, 299, 300, 2509, 2512, 2513, 2514, 2525, 2527, 307, 308, 2532, 282, 295, 296, 301, 302, 2517, 2.28, 286, 290, 2516, 2020, 2509, 2506, 281, 287, 280, 244, 287, 2544, 2507, 4167,  4171, 4172, 2521, 2523, 2527, 2529, 2530, 2531, 2532, 2540, 2546, 2548, 2555, 2556, 613, 615, 616, 619, 621, 622 and 625 of R.S. Khatian No. 136 (M.R.R. Khatian No. 191) having a Jama of Taka 75.25 of Mouza Tetiai P.S. Cox's Bazar to appellant O.Ps. 1-5 Sultan Ahmed, Syed Nur, Gura Mia, Badar Alain and Sarnuda Khatun of village Tetia, P.S. Cox's Bazar for Taka 1,00 000/- by a deed of sale (Ext. 1) executed and registered on 27.4.79 in the Chittagong Sadar Sub-Registrar's Office. Late Barada Prasad Rakshit, father of vendors Jyoti Prasad and Tarun Tapan had purchased the case land in 1941, Pre-emptee respondents 1-3 and other respondents 4-67 are co-sharers in the holding by inheritance and purchase. Transferors Jyoti Prasad and Tarun Tapan transferred the land in question without the knowledge of the pre-emptee respondents. and without serving any notice upon them. Appellant pre-emptee 1-4 and P.W. 2 Ula Mia used to cultivate the case land for 10/15 years as bargadars under Barada Prasad Rakshit and after latter's death under the vendors who are the heirs of Barada Prasad Rakshit. Pre-emptee appellants 1-5 are strangers to case land. P.W.2 Ula Mia used to cultivate three kanis of case land as bargadar. When as usual P.W.2 Ula Mia also wanted to cultivate the case land, pre-emptee appellants 1.4 . did not allow him to cultivate the case land stating that they had themselves purhased the same. On 1st Ashar 1388 B.S. corresponding to 16.6.81 A.D. the pre-emptor Respondents 1-3 came to know from P.W.2 Ula Mia for the first time that the pre-emptee appellants had purchased the case land. Pre-emptor respondent No. 1 Mohammad Islam then tried to find out if any such kabala had been registered at Cox's Bazar Sub-Registrar's Office or at Patiya Sub-Registrar's Office. Failing to get any trace of any such kabala there he went to Chittagong. Sub-Registrar's Office and succeeded in obtaining a certified copy of the kabala on 24.6.81, To keep the sale secret the pre-emptees registered the kabala at Sadar, Chittagong. The pre-emptor respondents 1-3 thus coming to know about the transfer for the first time instituted the present case on 14.7.81 praying for pre-emption depositing the consideration money of Taka 1,00,000/, with compensation of Taka 10,000/- Pre-emptors are agriculturists. It was also asserted in the petition by the pre-emptors that if they are allowed to pre-empt the case land, the total quantity of Land after adding the case laud to the land held by them and their families shall not exceed the maximum ceiling of land allowable under the law (section 90 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act read with P.O. No: 98 of 1972). 

 6. Although in the written objection it was claimed that pre-emptee purchaser Gura Mia (0.P.W.1) was a co-sharer in the case holding, but, this contention was given up at the time of trial and O.P.W.1 stated in his evidence that subsequent to the present purchase the became co-sharer in the case holding by his purchase on the basis of kabala Ext. A dated 25.8.79. So, it is undisputed that he was not a co-sharer in the holding at the time of the present sale. It is thus not disputed that the pre-emptees are stranger purchasers in the case holding. It is also not disputed that the land sought to be pre-empted is the entire land transferred by the vendors to the pre-emptees by the registered kabala dated 27.4.79 (Ext 1.) 

 8. On behalf of the pre-emptors three local witnesses were examined apart from a formal witness, namely PW 4 Advocate Samar Kamal. They also exhibited the disputed Kabala Ext.l and the plaint Ext 2. filed by the pre-emptees 1-5 against the Government and others in O.S. No. 237 of 1981 in the Court of Munsif, Cox's Bazar which was admitted by O.P.W 1 Gura Mia (pre-emptee No.3). P.W. 1 Mohammad Islam states that no notices of transfer were sent to the preemptors. OPW 1 Gura Mia (pre-emptee No. 3) stated that they gave notices to all co-sharers including pre-emptors. But in his cross-examination he stated that he cannot say whether the notices were served on co-sharers. It is therefore clear that the pre-emptors who are undisputedly co-sharers were not notified. 

 9. PW 1 Mohammad Islam stated that the pre-emptees 1-5 did not tell them (the pre-emptors) about the purchase of case land at any time, that the pre-emptees 1-4 were bargadars in the case land under the original owners, that for the first time he came to know of the purchase of the case land by the pre-emptees from PW.2 Ula Mia on 16.6.81 corresponding to Ist Ashar, 1388 B.S., that he was never the 'karmakarak' of the vendors that the pre-emptees 1-5 built a salt godown in the case land during the pendency of present case and that thereafter at their instance a local inspection was held. In his cross-examination' he denied the defence version of the case. 

 10. PW 2 Ula Mia stated that he was a bargadar of three kanis of the case land under the vendors, that pre-emptees 1-5 were also bargadars of the case land for 10/11 years under the vendors and that when he came to know about the sale by the vendors to the pre-emptees he reported the fact to P.W. 1 Mohammad Islam on 1st Ashar 1388 B.S. In cross-examination he denied the defence suggestion that P.W. 1 Mohammad Islam was the 'karmakarak' in respect of the case land on behalf of the sellers and that he was falsely deposing at the instance of P.W. 1 Mohammad Islam. 

 11. P.W. 3 Matiur Rahman is an independent witness. He states that he has land near the case land, that emptees 1-4 and P.W. 2 Ula Mia used to possess the case land as bargadar under the vendors for the last 11 years, that there was no godown in the ease land for keeping salt and that in the previous Jaista only the pre-emptees raised a godown in the case land. He denied the defence suggestion that P.W. 1 Mohammad Islam used to look after the case land on behalf of the original owners and that he is bargadar of P.W. 1 Mohammad 

 13. C.P.W. 1 Gura Mia states that P.W. Mohammad Islam used to look after the case land on behalf of the original owners, that P.W. 1 could not Purchase the case land as he was short of fund, that P.W. 1 settled the price of the case land and was present at the time of registration of the impugned kabala dated 27.4.79, that P.W. 1 delivered possession of the case land to the pre-emptees on behalf of the original owners, that 2 kanis out of the case land are salt land and .the rest are paddy land, that pre-emptees are possessing the case land, Thai the son of pre-emptor. No. 2, is the. Manager of the irrigation scheme of the three kanis of case land, that they built a salt godown in the case land 15/20 days after the present kabala. He denied the suggestion that the pre-emptees were in possession of the case land as bargadar before from the purchase to the original owners. In cross-examination he admitted that he cannot say whether notices were served on the co-Sharers. He also that the vendors who are sons of Barada Prasad Rakshit sold their entire interests in the holding to them. Thus it is clear that the vendors had no subsisting interest in the case holding O.P.W. 1 Gura Mia claimed that pre-emptor P.W 1 Mohammad Islam was present at the time of execution and registration of the kabala in the Sub-Registrar's Office at Chittagong but the kabala Ext. 1 shows that P.W. 1 Mohaminad Islam was not attesting witness in the kabala. When O.P.W. 1 Gura Mia contends that pre-emptor P.W. 1 Mohammad Islam was the caretaker of the case land and that it is at his instance that the purchase by the pre emptees from the vendors was negotiated and the, kabala was executed and registered, in the normal circumstances there is no reason why pre-emptor P.W. 1 Mohammad Islam's signature as attesting witness should not be in the kabala. This fact eloquently shows that pre-emptor P.W. 1 Mohammad Islam was neither the 'karmakarak' of the vendors nor the negotiator of the present purchase nor was he present at the time of execution and registration O.P.W. 1 Gura Mia admitted that he along with other pre-emptees filed the plaint (EXt. 2) in C.S. No. 237 of 1981 in the Court of Munsif, Cox's Bazar against the Government (S.D.O. Cox's Bazar) and another  (Zakir Hossain) in which pre-emptees 1-5 were the plaintiffs. Pre-emptees as plaintiffs filed that suit for a decree declaring inter alia that the Suit land is not a vested property. In that plaint the pre-emptees 1-5 had stated in para 3, "That, the said Barada and his sons used to live at Patiya and they possessed the land through the plaintiffs as tenants. These plaintiffs as tenants of said Barada and his sons have been in peaceful possession. The said Jyoti and Tarun Tapan for want of money sold their right and title to the plaintiffs vide kabala dated 27.4.79". 

 14. There was no controversy on the issue that a party's previous statement regarding a fact in issue is relevant under section 21 of the Evidence Act and can .be used against him if he has not appeared in the witness box at all. But previously there was some controversy as to whether a party's previous admission can be used against him without drawing his attention to it in accordance with the provision of section 145 of the Evidence Act when the party is in the witness box. Contrary views on this point were expressed for example in Malek Desraj Vs. Tiara 1946 Lahore 65 (PB) and Ajodhya V. Bhawani, A.I.R. 1957 Allahabad page 1 (FB). But now it is well settled that even if the party appearing in the witness box is not confronted with his contrary previous admission, his such previous admission if duly proved is admissible. This view finds support in the case of Bharat Vs. Bhagirathi, A.LR. 1966 (SC) 402 wherein it was observed, "Admissions duly proved are admissible evidence irrespective of whether the party making them appeared in the witness box or not and whether that party when appearing as witness was confronted with these statements is case it made statement contrary to those admissions." 

 15. Faced with this admission made by the pre-emptees in the plaint Ext. 2 of the said suit that they were in possession of the case land from before their purchase on 27.4.79, it appears that op. 23.3.83 the plaintiffs of that suit i.e. the present pre-emptees 1-5 withdrew their suit under. Order 23, rule 1 C.P.C. and the pre-emptees were permitted to withdraw from the suit with liberty to institute a fresh suit if not otherwise barred under the law. But, in spite of such withdrawal from a suit admissions made by the parties therein are admissible in evidence. The view finds support in P.L.D. 1975 Karachi 509 There is thus no truth in the present statement of the pre-emptees that they started possessing by the pre-emptees regarding the case land from the date of present transfer on 27.4.79. Since it appears that the pre-emptees were in possession of the case land from long before the present purchase and deed of transfer Ext. 1 was registered neither at Cox's Bazar Sub-Registrar's Office, Sadar, Chittagong, it is evident that it was not possible for the pre-emptors to know anything about the present transfer. O.P.W.1 Gura Mia admitted that he had no paper to show that pre-emptor P.W.1 Mohammad Islam vs, as caretaker of the case land under the original owners. There is thus no truth in the story that pre-emptor P.W.1 Mohammad Islam was the caretaker of the case land on behalf of the vendors. He also admitted that he cannot produce any paper to show that the son of pre-emptee No. 2 is the Manager of irrigation scheme of the three kanis land of the case land. This also indicate that there is no truth in this statement. 

 16. We have already shown that O.P.W.2, O.P.W.3, O.P.W. 4, O.P.W. 5 and O.P.W.6 are all highly interested witnesses. They all stated that pre-emptees we are possessing the case land since 1979. From the discussion of the evidence of O.P.W. 1 Gura Mia read with admission made by the pre-emptees in the plaint Ext. 2 of other Suit No. 237 of 1981 it is clear that the pre-emptecs were in possession of the case land as bargadars under the vendors from long before the present sale in 1979 O.P.W. 2 Mohammad Hussain and O.P.W. 3 Fazal Rahman stated that petitioner No. 1 used to possess the case land before 1979. This statement of these two witnesses is not even supported by any other witness including O.P.W. 1 Gura Mia who merely tried to contend that pre-emptor No. 1 Mohammad Islam was a care-taker. As already shown, there is no truth in the contention that pre-emptor No.1 Mohammad Islam was caretaker of the case land on behalf of the vendors. There is also no reason to hold that the pre-emptor No. 1 Mohammad Islam possessed the case land before pre-emptees 1-5 started possessing in 1979 after purchase, The statements of the O.P.Ws. that after purchasing the case land the pre-emptees built a salt go-down in 1979 are also untrue. P. W. 3 Matiur Rahman who is an independent witness stated on. 1.3.83 that the pre-emptees raised a godown in the case land in the previous Jaistha. Thus it appears that the salt go-down in question was erected during the pendency of the present case. In view of the above discussion of the evidence on record we had that the pre-emptor co-sharers who were not notified came to know of the present sale by the vendors in favour of the pre-emptees for the first time on 16.6.81 on which date they heard about the matter from P.W. 2 Ula Mia. The present case was instituted on 14.7.81. The case is therefore not barred by limitation. 

 17. Mr. A.K.M. Shafiqur Rahman submits that as the assertion of the pre-emptors in respect of the requirement of section 90 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 read with P.O. No. 98 of 1972 that if the case land is allowed to be pre-empted, the added land will not exceed the maximum ceiling fixed by law for the pre-emptors has been denied in the written objection and as there is no evidence on behalf of the pre-emptors in support of their assertion in this respect, the application for pre-emption is liable to be dismissed on that ground. In the present case the assertion of the three pre-emptors made in the application that if they are allowed to pre-empt the land the total land held by them will not exceed the maximum ceiling of land allowed by law to be held by them was denied in para 10 of the written objection in the following words: 

 "The statements of the petitioners that they are agriculturists, that there is no legal bar for them to pre-emptee that the cause of action arose on 24.6.81 etc. is false, fraudulent, baseless, motivated and harassing and all their statements arc directly denied by the opposite parties." 

 The denials are evasive, vague and uncertain. Even if such an evasive and vague denial is treated to be at best a general denial, it is certainly not a specific denial and the pre-emptees did not deal specifically with this assertion of fact of which they do not admit the truth. The pre-emptees evasively stated that it is not correct that there is no legal bar for them to pre-empt. The pre-emptees did not specifically allege that if the pre-emption application is allowed, the added land would exceed the permissible limit of land allowable under the law by the three pre-emptors to be held. In this connection a reference may be made to the decision is the case of Shahidur Rahman Molla & others Vs, Abdul Halim Molla & others, 35 DLR 79. 

 "(3) It shall not be sufficient for a defendant in his written statement to deny generally the grounds alleged by the plaintiff, but the defendant must deal specifically with each allegation of fact of which he does not admit the truth, except damages. 

 (5) Every allegation of fact in the plaint if not denied specifically or by necessary implication, or stated to be not admitted in the pleading of the defendant, shall be taken to be admitted except as against a person under disability: 

 18. Section 141 C.P.C. provides that the procedure provided in the C.P.C. in regard to suits shall be followed, as far as it can be made applicable, in all proceedings in any Court of Civil jurisdiction. The above quoted provisions of Orders 8 and 14 there-fore apply to the present proceeding. As already stated, the pre-emptees in the instant case gave general denial but did not specifically deny the assertion of the pre-emptors regarding the question of maximum ceiling of land and did not specifically allege that if the pre-emption application is allowed, the added land would exceed the permissible limit. Therefore it is not a sufficient denial in terms of Order 8 rule 3 C.P.C. The rule in Order 8, rule 5 is known as the doctrine of non-traverse which means that where a material averment is passed over by evasive denial without a specific denial, it is taken to admitted. Thus the material proposition of fact affirmed by the pre-emptors regarding the fact that if the pre-emption is allowed, the added land will not exceed the ceiling of land the pre-emptor are permitted to hold under the law has not been specifically and sufficiently denied by the pre-emptees. Therefore in terms of rule 1 (1) and rule 1 (3) of Order 14 C.P.C. there was no issue before the trial Court nor this Court is required to give any finding in respect of ceiling of land in the absence of any specific averment to the contrary. There is thus no substance in the argument of the learned Advocate for the pre-emptees that the application for pre-emption is liable to be rejected as the pre-emptors did not adduce any evidence in support of their assertion regarding the ceiling of land because, as already stated, there is absence of specific averment to the Contrary. In this connection a reference may be made to the decision in, the case of Md. Matiur Rahman Vs. Md. Iman Ali @ Md. Iman Miah & others, 1981 B.L. D. (A.D.) . 280 Wherein it has been held that mere omission to make an assertion in respect of ceiling of land in the application by the pre-emptors, or to adduce evidence to this effect in the absence of any averment to the contrary wily not render the application liable to be dismissed and  record a finding to this effect in such a Stance cannot be a ground for dismissal of the pre-emption case. 

 20. Mr. A.K.M. Shafiqur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the pre-emptee appellants referred to the ease. of Abdus Samad & others Vs, Sohrab Ali & others 33 DLR (A.D.) 113 wherein it has been observed: "However, the special statutory Provision in sub-section (2) or section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as to the necessary parties to be impleaded is mandatory................Of course, in an appropriate case such objection May be to be raised in the appeal. This may be done on the ground that the appeal is continuation of the suit or proceeding."'
